title: Everyone Is Looking for You
logline: Two days in January: a wall full of Youngstown, an empty shelf, a disaster on a car radio, and a card table on the Commons where everybody meets everybody.

previously.text: On the wall at the Point before Christmas, Lena, from a letter she knows by heart: *“Do you remember what she was wearing? The police said a jean jacket. They never found it. Her grandmother made the patch.”*
At Santa Barbara she was waiting at the rope with a sign in eyeliner: OFFICIALLY. By the belt, a girl from your flight had her phone up, sideways, very steady.
Lena, landing: *“Come find me tomorrow, Youngstown.”* You wrote back: *tell laney a king cake is a carry on*
At a gas station in Buellton you called your mother first. “You were on that phone with Lena all break.” “She’s still got a boyfriend, Ma. He wrote a song for her. It was good.”
At Hale’s table, Lena: “Hi, Jack. Happy New Year.” Then Dido. Hale: “Carthage is not on the syllabus. Kindly leave it there.”
In the Fishbowl, Doug Pruitt: “Dude. This is like when you and Lena do it.” Skye picked a thread off your sleeve.

body: January sun comes in low across the quad at twenty past seven and lands on Theo’s half of 412: the made bed, the shoes in their line under it, the orange hat hung on the bedpost by its brim. Theo stands in the middle of it at the mirror on the inside of the closet door, knotting a tie for the Sigma Rho rush breakfast. The navy blazer is already on and buttoned. He wears it like a dare.
On the dresser his iPhone buzzes, quits, and buzzes again. Theo finishes the knot, looks at it, takes it apart and starts over.
“Brooks,” he says. “Brooks Callahan would like me to know that eggs are at eight. He has told me three times since six. That’s leadership.”

Jack is on the edge of his own bed with one shoe on. Theo picks the phone up off the dresser, wakes it, and turns to face the room, and this morning he reads Jack his own wall first, which he can see, being a friend, and then the News Feed, in the voice: the lector at the twelve-ten doing the intentions, slow, a little through the nose, every name given its full weight.

body: He turns the phone around and holds it out across the gap between the beds, so Jack can see it at the size it is: a candle stuck upright in a dinner roll, and behind it Lena in the gray cardigan, smiling at whoever held the camera, and Julian’s arm along the back of her chair.

“For Julian Park-Ellis,” Theo reads, “who had a birthday.” He touches the likes open and reads them down, without inflection. “Tess Broussard Fontenot. Laney Price. Remy Broussard. Kenzie Rourke. Peter Haddad.” And nine more Jack has never heard of, each in the same voice, to the end of the list. “Lord, hear our prayer.”
Jack has the shoelace in both hands.
Friday she said *call me after*, and Monday night he didn’t.

Theo turns the phone back to himself. “For the rush committee of Sigma Rho,” he reads off nothing at all, “which meets over eggs at eight to decide my worth.” A pause, for the congregation. “Lord, hear our prayer.”

The phone goes into the inside pocket of the blazer. He goes back to the mirror and tightens a knot that doesn’t need it, and in the glass his eyes find Jack’s and go back to the knot. He has been like this since Sunday night: courteous, exact, a host with a houseguest he happens to like. No *Father Jack*. No second congratulations. Not a word about the girl with the three hundred and ninety-one.
“Rush,” Theo says, “is a job interview where they also throw you in a pool.”
“You want it?” Jack says.

Theo looks at the knot in the glass. “Yes,” he says. And, at more length: “They have a house on the bluff, a chef named Hector who does omelets to order on Sundays, and a composite photograph in the front hall going back to 1971 in which no one has ever smiled. I’d be the first.”
“Are they throwing you in a pool?”

“Costigan. It’s January. They’re throwing me in the *ocean*. Brooks has a wetsuit for the ones they like.” He turns the collar of the blazer up, looks at it, turns it down. At the door, at twenty-eight past: “Eggs and judgment.”
When he’s gone, Jack says it for him, under his breath. “Lord, hear our prayer.”
The RAZR goes on the desk at 7:31. It’s half past ten at Ursuline, between periods.

body: Ma’s can has been on his desk since Saturday night, beside the lamp, where it’s the first thing he sees: the Café du Monde can, empty, washed, the lid pressed back on. He picks it up. He stands on the desk chair with it, the chair swiveling a little under him, to put it on the top shelf of the closet, where he won’t see it every morning.

The shelf runs the width of the closet, split down the middle by a plywood divider somebody put in before either of them was born. His half is bare. He sets the can on it, and from up on the chair he can see over the divider onto Theo’s: the gray camera bag; the shoebox, COOKIES — DON’T; the crook of the Burberry hooked over the front edge. At the back, where the black duffel sat all fall, the dust has kept its shape, a clean rectangle with the corners worn round. There is nothing else.

In September, at ten past one in the morning, a jean jacket came up out of a black bag into his hands, Our Lady on the back. On the morning of the first storm in December, a red Ferris wheel on a collar, two inches of it, where a zipper had come open. The week before Christmas, at two in the morning on the wall at the Point, Lena, with a letter she had by heart: *They never found it.* This morning: a gray camera bag, a shoebox, an umbrella, and a clean place in the dust.

s02.slug: TUESDAY · 9:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE MAILBOXES
body: The mailboxes on two are a wall of little brass doors, each with a window the size of a stamp and a combination nobody remembers past October, and the radiator under them knocks twice and thinks about a third. Down the hall somebody shuffles toward the showers in slippers, and a hair dryer starts up behind a door and stops. Jack is down from four with his bag on his shoulder and twenty minutes before a nine-thirty, and Lena and Laney are ahead of him at the wall.

Laney has her sunglasses on indoors and the Pi Lam hood up. Lena is in the navy peacoat buttoned to the top, her hair up off her neck with a pencil through it, and she has a yellow package slip from the front desk in both hands and is reading it.
Laney sees him first. She turns to her mailbox and opens it, and takes out nothing, and studies that through the sunglasses.
Lena reads the slip to the bottom, the fine print too, before she looks up.
“Morning, Jack.”
“Morning.”
She folds the slip in half, and in half again. “How was the rest of your break?”

She heard most of it on the phone already, every night of it, from the garage. She lets him tell it again like news. He starts with Saturday: three sandwiches in foil by the front door, labeled in Ma’s capitals, PITTSBURGH TO DENVER, DENVER TO SANTA BARBARA, IN CASE, because the airlines don’t feed you. Nonna going through the housedress for the twenty, left pocket, right pocket, left again, a butterscotch, a holy card, *per il viaggio*. Rosie’s drawing of the plane, with the crab belted into the next seat, on the aisle, in case. Pop at the Departures curb, *thirty seconds*, and still there with the hazards going when Jack looked back through the glass, explaining something to a man in a vest.
“How’s her hand?” Lena says. It’s the question you ask.
“Better. She found the twenty with it.”
“Good.”

He tells the rest well. He knows where the laughs are in it; he has told her worse things better, at two in the morning, and had her laughing till she had to put the phone down. She listens with the slip folded small in her fingers and her eyes on his collar.
“And Ma says to tell you it was good coffee.” He hears how it sounds and adds the rest. “She said to use those words.”
Lena looks at him properly, the first time this morning. “Tell her I’m glad.”
Laney shuts her mailbox.
Then Denver, and a man from Grand Junction who fell asleep on his shoulder somewhere over Kansas and woke up apologizing and kept apologizing until Colorado —
And he stops. He got as far as Denver.
She doesn’t ask for the rest. “That sounds lovely, Jack.”

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first.

body: The Anacapa waffle irons are going down the line like a drum corps that has never rehearsed, each one finishing on its own beep, and the tray belt by the dish window rattles forks away into the back of the building. Doug Pruitt has taken the end of the long table by the glass by opening a laptop on it, which is how he takes everything.
Theo comes in last, still in the navy Sigma Rho blazer, with a banana and a glass of water on his tray. His breath reaches the table about a second ahead of him.

“Brooks Callahan,” he says, sitting, “handed me a raw onion at eight-twenty this morning. Not as a gesture. A yellow onion, skin on, in front of the entire lacrosse team, who stopped chewing.” He peels the banana. “Brooks says it builds character. I ate it like an apple, and it built breath.”

Kevin has divided his tray by macronutrient, chicken and egg and cottage cheese in a tidy triptych, and is explaining to Margot that thirty grams a meal is the number. She has not asked. “So the body,” Margot says, over a coffee she takes black as a position, “converts cottage cheese into opinions.”
“Basically,” Kevin says, cheerfully, and eats the egg.
“Dude,” Doug says, scrolling ESPN with one finger. “Pete Carroll is going to *Seattle*. It rains there, dude. It rains *on purpose*.”
“My father had lunch with him in November,” Theo says. “He ordered for him.”
Doug opens his mouth, looks at Theo’s face, and shuts it. The banana goes on being peeled.
“And McGwire,” Doug tries, recovering. “All those years, and now he’s *sorry*. He’s sorry he got caught.”
“He’s sorry in the passive voice,” Margot says.
“Mistakes were made,” says Theo, “by a younger, larger man.”
“Laney would’ve *loved* this,” Doug says. “Where’s Laney?”
“Laney has a mandatory Pi Lam luncheon,” Theo says. “Chicken salad. They take attendance by photograph.”
Margot looks at Theo. Theo looks at the banana.
Theo’s iPhone lights on his tray. He reads it without picking it up, and slides it under the banana peel.
“Laney,” he says, “would like me to know that the chicken salad is excellent, and that she is sitting with people who understand what the Like button means.”

Doug works it out last. “Dude. You *liked* it?” He scrolls up the wall to the status and finds it, and turns the laptop so the table can see the little blue thumb with the names after it. Theo Vance, first.
“I like a great many things, Pruitt. It’s a reflex. I liked the Pope in Cameroon.” Theo eats a piece of banana. “I have been informed it was not a reflex. I have been informed it was a position.”

Doug swings the laptop toward Jack. “Okay. Okay okay okay. I have to do the wall.” Jack’s profile is open on it. Doug friended everyone on the fourth floor in September, and since nine this morning, by his own account, he has been reading Jack’s wall in the back of Psych 1 with the sound off. “I’m going to read it,” he says, “as a public service.”

body: Morro Hall 1100 is the big one on the south end of campus, three hundred and twelve seats raked up from a stage the size of a two-car garage, every seat bolted to a fold-down desk the width of a paperback, and at five to eleven it smells of wet sweatshirts and somebody’s breakfast burrito. Oceanography 1 fills the science requirement for everybody who looked at Chemistry and saw their life flash before their eyes. On the fourth floor it is called Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Jack signed up for it in November at seven in the morning, on the Fishbowl computer, a minute after Hale’s seminar and before the Biology sections filled, because it met twice a week and nobody had ever failed it.

In December, on the phone from Glenwood Avenue, a week after she asked him, for no reason, what he’d signed up for in the spring, Skye told him she’d picked a science and wouldn’t tell him which. *It’s a surprise. Surprises are good for you. Ask anybody.*

He comes in the side door at the top of the hall, and she is in the last row, in the corner seat by the wall, under the exit sign, in sunglasses and a gray Marisol hoodie with the hood up, like a person who would very much like not to be recognized and has dressed for it in exactly what guarantees it. Her feet are up on the seat in front. The seat beside her has a textbook on it, saving it. She lifts the book when she sees him and holds it up beside her face — *Oceanography 1*, eleventh edition, a wave on the cover — and does not smile, and then does.
“Surprise,” she says. “I took a science.”
“You took my science.”

“I took *a* science. You happen to be in it.” She moves the book to her lap. “I surf. I wanted to know what’s hitting me. And I wanted to sit in the back of something with you where my agent can’t call me. Both things can be true. Sit. You’re blocking the exit, and that’s a fire code.”
He sits. The fold-down desk on his side is carved, very small, with somebody’s initials and a date in 1994 and a wave somebody drew to go with it.

Dr. Dale Fenner comes onto the stage at eleven exactly in Tevas and a fleece vest and a sunburn on top of a sunburn, with a coffee cup the size of a vase. He has the look of a man who would rather be in a boat and has made his peace with not being in one twice a week. He doesn’t introduce himself. He puts up a slide of the earth from space, mostly blue, and stands next to it with his coffee.

“Seventy-one percent,” he says. “And we have better maps of Mars.” He lets that sit. “This semester you’re going to learn why the water’s salty, why the beach you’re sitting on in February won’t be there in August, why there are waves, which some of you care about very much” — a few whoops from the middle rows, and Skye, under her breath, *one of us* — “and what the ground is doing under all of it. Which is moving. The ground is not where you left it. Week two.”
The syllabus comes up the rows in stacks. Skye takes two and hands him one, and he reads it while Fenner talks, like a lease.

body.title: OCEANOGRAPHY 1 — Introduction to the Ocean · Spring 2010
body.text:
Dr. D. Fenner · TTh 11:00–12:15 · Morro Hall 1100
Three midterms (25%) · Final (30%) · Term project (20%) · Sections (25%)
TERM PROJECT: pairs, assigned by seat on Thursday. You keep your partner till May. No trades. I have heard every reason.

body: Under it, in pencil, before he has finished the paragraph, she has drawn a small arrow from *pairs* to the seat he’s sitting in.
“Till May,” he says, low.

“Till May.” She doesn’t look at him. She looks at Fenner, attentive as a front-row girl, with her pencil on the arrow. “I read ahead. I’m very prepared. I’m going to be an incredible partner, Jack Costigan. You’re going to have to carry nothing. I’m going to carry you up the beach like a lifeguard in a calendar.”
“Which month?”
“July,” Skye says. “Obviously.”

For an hour and a quarter they behave about as well as the back row of anything behaves. She draws in his margin. He draws in hers — a wave, then a worse wave. She writes *is fenner single* and he writes *hes married to a boat* and she writes *arent we all* and caps her pen on it, very pleased. When Fenner says *bathymetry* she writes it down in capitals and then, under it, *what*. When he explains the ocean is layered, warm on top and cold and heavy underneath, and the layers don’t like to mix, she moves her knee over against his under the little desk, and writes *science* in his margin and underlines it twice.

At half past, Fenner turns the lights down for a video from a wave tank at Scripps: a long glass channel, a paddle at one end pushing water down it in slow, perfect swells, and three hundred people go quiet in the dark. Skye watches it with her chin on her fist. On the screen a swell reaches the slope built into the far end of the tank, and stands up, and curls, and comes apart.

“That’s it,” she says, very low. “That’s all it is. It feels the bottom and it trips.” She doesn’t look away from the screen. “Every wave I ever fell off of, that’s what it was doing. I’ve been falling off physics.”
“You didn’t know a wave trips?”
“Sol said it was the ocean’s mood.” Her knee again, under the desk. “Sol thinks everything is a mood. Sol thinks the toaster has a mood.”

When the lights come up she has written across the bottom of his syllabus, in capitals, WAVE FEELS BOTTOM → TRIPS, and under it a stick figure going over the front of a wave with its arms up, labeled ME, and a second stick figure on the sand with a book, labeled YOU (NOT HELPING).
It is the first room on campus he has walked into since August without his eyes going, on their own, to look for a pencil through somebody’s hair.

Somebody in the room knows *her*, though. A girl in the row below turns halfway around in her seat with her iPhone up, and holds it at an angle that is supposed to look like she is checking the time, and the little fake shutter sound goes off in the quiet while Fenner is drawing a thermocline. Skye doesn’t take the sunglasses off. She lifts two fingers off the desk at the girl, a small wave, the kind you give a car that let you in.
“She’ll get a better one if you look at me,” she says, without moving her mouth much.
At the end Fenner says Thursday, seats, partners, and don’t come to me about it, and the hall stands up all at once with the noise of three hundred and twelve desks folding.

s03.slug: TUESDAY · 1:15 PM · THE SOCCER STADIUM OVERFLOW LOT, CSU MARISOL
s03.music: The Ting Tings — “Shut Up and Let Me Go”
body: January sun comes flat across the overflow lot behind the soccer stadium: eleven acres of white lines painted for game days, light poles throwing short shadows at a quarter past one, and in the middle of it the Saab with its top down, the only car on the asphalt. Her iPod is plugged into the tape deck through the adapter, the cord looped once around the gearshift, and the Ting Tings are coming out of the door speakers louder than a car this old was built to take.

She has wanted to teach him stick since December. The Saab is a manual, and everything Jack has ever driven — his father’s Silverado, the driver’s-ed Taurus at Mooney with a second brake on the passenger side — has shifted for him. Skye is sideways in the passenger seat in his flannel over a tank top, sunglasses pushed up into her hair, feet up on the dash with her toes against the windshield, giving instruction.

“Clutch is the one on the left. You let it out like you’re giving somebody bad news,” she says. “Slow, slow, and then all at once, and then you don’t apologize.” She holds up a finger. “House rule. Every time you stall, you owe me a voice. My choice.”
“What kind of voice?”
“Whoever I say. I’ll know if you phone it in.”
He stalls in eleven feet. The Saab bucks once, as if it’s been insulted, and dies, and the Ting Tings carry on without it.

“A Teamster taught me,” she says, “on the Warner lot, in a grip truck, when I was fourteen. I stalled it twenty times and he never said anything. He just ate his sandwich.” She turns the music down a hair. “I am not that man.”
“So,” Skye says. “First voice. Your father.”

All she knows of his father is his airport impression — the arm out, the squint, the face doing nothing — so he gives her the rest: Pop in the recliner, reviewing the Rose Bowl. The chin down, the eyes on a television in Ohio, the voice up out of the bottom of a lunch pail. “Pryor.”
“That’s not the squint,” Skye says. “The squint was better at the airport. Two. Out of ten.”
The second stall is Hale, from the description. “Costigan,” Jack says, all cut glass, “you have buggered the clutch, and I confess myself unsurprised.”
“That’s a pirate. Hale isn’t a pirate. Three, for *buggered*.”

For the third she wants the Pope blessing the Saab, and he says he isn’t doing a blessing for a bit, and she puts both hands up — “Fine, fine, he doesn’t bless it, he just *notices* it” — so he gives her Benedict XVI, gentle and Bavarian, confronted with a dented convertible in a parking lot, without a word: hands folded at the waist, head a little to one side, a long, mild look down the length of the fender.
She laughs out loud and slaps the dash. “He looks so *sorry* for it. I’d watch that Pope.”
Four is Nonna, and he doesn’t have to think about it. “*Piano, piano*,” he says, with one hand going in a small circle over the wheel, the way hers goes over a pot.
“What’s it mean?”
“Slowly. Slowly.”
“Then why didn’t you?” She gives him a six. Nonna is his best, she tells him, and he is not allowed to get cocky about a woman who is eighty-four.
Five is Corinne. He narrows his eyes and works an invisible BlackBerry with his thumb: “Is that *employable*?”

“Wait.” Skye takes her phone off the dash. “You should hear the original.” She finds a voicemail from nine this morning and puts it on speaker, and holds it out between them over the gearshift, and Beverly Hills comes into the overflow lot, clipped and low.
“Skye. Corinne. About Sunday. That was a sighting we didn’t manage, and I’m not upset — I want to be very clear that I’m not upset. We’re going to let it breathe. Nothing new goes up. Call me.”

Skye deletes it with her thumb. “One. She’d fire you.” She lays the phone on her knee and takes her feet off the dash. “She wants to let it breathe,” she says. “I’m going to let it breathe in front of everybody.”

After that the stalls come faster. Six is Theo — “Costigan, I owe you a kidney” — and she gives it a seven: “You’ve studied.” Seven is Gina screaming at a DVD, and Skye gives it a five for volume. Eight is Doug Pruitt, *dude* stretched over five vowels until it comes apart, and she gives it a nine and makes him do it again just to hear it. Nine is her mother.
“Jack. *Jack.* Sit, sit, sit.”
Skye pulls her sunglasses down over her eyes. “Ten,” she says, from behind them. “Never again. I mean it.”

By then his left foot has found it: the place in the pedal’s travel where the clutch takes hold, a small shiver up through the sole of his shoe that means the car is listening. He gets her rolling in first along the painted lines, past one light pole and the next, and the engine climbs, and he pushes in and pulls the stick down and back and lets out, and the Saab goes into second like it was waiting to be asked. It doesn’t buck. It goes. Skye screams like he’s won a car on a game show.

She makes him bring it to a stop at the far fence — badly, but a stop — and comes across the console with the sunglasses knocked crooked and kisses him, one kiss, hers, with both fists in the front of his shirt, and sits back. “That’s the prize,” she says. “There’s only the one. Don’t get used to it.”
The song has gone around to the start again. She looks at him from her side of the car with her knees up.
“I’d like you to stall again.”
“I just learned not to.”
“I know.” She doesn’t blink. “I’d like to see what you look like when you do it on purpose.”
So he lets the clutch out too fast, on purpose, with his eyes on her, and the Saab shudders and quits against the fence.
“That one doesn’t count,” Skye says. “That one’s a gift.”
She reaches over and puts her hand over his on the knob, and with the other hand she gets out the white iPhone.

She holds it out at arm’s length across the console with its back to him, the one eye on his side of the car, where she can’t see the screen and doesn’t try. The shutter makes its fake little sound. Again. On the third he’s laughing — at her, at the phone, at the idea of himself in a picture — and she brings it in and looks. “That one.”
It’s him in her driver’s seat in the January light, laughing at something out of the frame, his hand still on the knob. He can’t remember what he was laughing at. It was her.
She types with her thumb, the tip of her tongue in the corner of her mouth, without asking him, and turns the phone around when it’s done.

body: “Corinne said nothing new goes up,” Jack says.
“Corinne said a lot of things.” She drops the phone in the cup holder, face up, and swings her feet over the console into his lap, and the subject is closed.

She has other news anyway, off her phone, and tells it like gossip about a cousin. Conan O’Brien put out a statement today; she read it before she picked him up. NBC wants Leno back at 11:35 and *The Tonight Show* pushed to five minutes after midnight, and Conan won’t do it. He says he won’t be the one to move it out of the hour it’s had since before either of them was born, because it would hurt the show.
“It’s very well written,” Skye says. “Somebody good was up all night.”
“Good for him,” Jack says. “They promised him that show.”
“Did they?”
“Two thousand four. Leno said it on his own show: in five years, it’s Conan’s. On the air, in front of everybody. That’s a promise. A promise is a promise.”

“NBC never promised Conan anything.” She counts it off with her toes against his thigh. “A network promised a time slot. Time slots aren’t people. In my business you can’t promise anybody anything — that’s what contracts are for. A contract is what everybody signs once everybody in the room has agreed not to mean it.”
“That’s bleak, Skye.”

“Ask Letterman. Carson retires, and everybody in Burbank thinks Letterman was promised that chair, and Letterman thinks so too, and Leno gets it because Leno was standing closest to the door.” She shrugs with her feet. “So Letterman goes to CBS and gets a lot of money in writing. That’s the happy ending. That’s the only kind we have.”
“Then Letterman should’ve got it in writing the first time.”
“*Thank* you.”
“It’s *healthy*. Everybody knows where they stand. At 12:05 everybody gets paid.” She tips her head back against the door frame and looks at him upside down. “And that’s what’s funny about Sunday.”
“So Sunday wasn’t a promise either.”
She brings her head up and looks at him the right way round.
“Sunday wasn’t to a network.”

choices.text: “So nobody in Burbank has ever meant anything.”
response: “So nobody in Burbank has ever meant anything.”

“Correct.” She pulls the sunglasses off to look at him properly, delighted to be pushed. “Welcome to my hometown. We have a parade. It’s mostly lawyers.” She pokes him in the ribs with her big toe. “Now get us out of this lot without killing it.”

choices.text: “You’re right. A time slot can’t keep a promise.”
response: “You’re right. A time slot can’t keep a promise.”

“Only people can.” She sits up and holds out her phone. “Say it again. I want it in writing.” So he types it into her notes with one finger, hunting for every letter on the glass, and she reads it back to him in Corinne, and saves it.

choices.text: “Leno’s chin is the only thing in Burbank anybody can count on.”
response: “Leno’s chin is the only thing in Burbank anybody can count on.”

She laughs so hard her heel catches the middle of the wheel and the horn goes off, one long bleat across eleven empty acres. “Horn’s a stall,” she says when she can. “House rule. I owe you.” So she does him — the shoulders up, the Youngstown in the vowels, the chin — and says it flat as Ohio: “I’m good.”

s03a.slug: TUESDAY · 2:31 PM · OCEAN ROAD, THE SAAB, PULLED OVER BY THE GROVE
body: At twenty past two she put him back behind the wheel for what she called the real exam, Ocean Road to the Grove and back without dropping out of second, and at the first stop sign her iPod died in the middle of a song, and the adapter slid out of the deck, and the Saab’s own radio came up by itself on KCLU in the dead air between programs.

Now he has it in second along the bluff with the Pacific on his left, doing twenty-five like a man carrying a cake, and the radio is somebody promising a gardening show at three, and Skye has one arm out of the car riding the wind up and down.

At 2:31 by the clock in the dash the program stops and the news comes in over it. A powerful earthquake has struck near Port-au-Prince, Haiti, this afternoon. The Geological Survey puts it at magnitude seven. There is no word yet on casualties. Telephone lines into the country are down. The man reading it says that part twice.

He pulls over. He does it badly, onto the dirt turnout under the first of the eucalyptus at the edge of the Grove, with his foot on the brake and nothing on the clutch, and the Saab jerks and stalls. Skye reaches across and turns the key the rest of the way off.

It’s quiet without the engine. Long strips of bark let go of the trees overhead and come down on the hood and the windshield. On the radio a man in Washington says he has been trying to reach people in Port-au-Prince since the shaking and can’t get through to anyone: not his office, not his family. There have been aftershocks already, the radio says, strong ones, minutes apart. It’s a city of a couple of million people. It is half past five there, and it will be dark soon.
Skye has brought her arm back into the car. She turns the volume down a notch, and then turns it back up to where it was.
“Where is Haiti,” she says. “Exactly.”
She doesn’t dress it up. She doesn’t know, and she says so, and waits.

“Under Cuba. Down and to the right.” He draws it on the dash with his finger, a shape like a claw reaching west. “It’s half an island. The other half’s the Dominican Republic. Port-au-Prince is on this side, in the bay.”
“How do you know that?”

“Rice Bowl.” Every Lent at St. Brigid’s they sent you home with a cardboard box you folded up yourself, Catholic Relief Services printed across the top, and you put your quarters in it instead of buying candy, and Ma handed them out at the office window on Ash Wednesday and took them back at Easter, heavy, rattling. There was a map on the side. Some years the map was Haiti. “Poorest country in our half of the world. They make you find it before you can do long division.”
Skye looks out through the windshield, past the bark on the glass, at the ocean, as though Haiti were somewhere out there and she might see it if she looked long enough.
“Two million,” Skye says, to herself, as though she is checking she heard it. “And they don’t know yet. Anything.”
“The radio doesn’t know yet either.”
A truck goes by on Ocean Road and the Saab rocks a little on its springs. On the radio the man reads it again from the top.

choices.text: *Cross yourself. Say the prayer out loud.*
choices.key: In the Saab, when the radio said Haiti, you crossed yourself and said a Hail Mary aloud. She asked for every word.
response: He crosses himself, forehead and heart and shoulders, there in the driver’s seat with his hands coming back to the wheel after, and says a Hail Mary, low, not hurrying it. Skye doesn’t look at the radio. She watches his mouth till he gets to the end.
“What was that?” she says. “The whole thing.”
He tells her, slowly, and she says the first half back to him: *Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you.* He gave it to her with *thee*. He doesn’t correct it.

At a quarter past three she takes the wheel back and drives him to his three-thirty with both hands on it, under the speed limit. At the curb on the Commons road she leans across and kisses him goodbye, short. “Text me when you’re out.” Her hand stays on his sleeve after the kiss, his cuff in her fingers, and then she lets go of it.

choices.key: In the Saab, when the radio said Haiti, you took her hand and turned the radio up.
response: He takes her hand off her knee and turns it palm up in his, and reaches over with the other and turns the radio up. They listen to the bulletin through to the end, and to the man in Washington again, and her thumb goes back and forth over his knuckles and doesn’t stop.

At a quarter past three she takes the wheel back and drives him to his three-thirty with both hands on it, under the speed limit. At the curb on the Commons road she leans across and kisses him goodbye, short. “Text me when you’re out.” Her hand stays on his sleeve after the kiss, his cuff in her fingers, and then she lets go of it.

choices.key: In the Saab, when the radio said Haiti, you told her your grandmother already had her rosary out.
response: “My nonna’s already got her rosary out,” he says. “I’d bet the car.”
“You don’t have a car.”
“Your car, then.”
She laughs, small, through her nose. After that she’s quiet, and they listen.

At a quarter past three she takes the wheel back and drives him to his three-thirty with both hands on it, under the speed limit. At the curb on the Commons road she leans across and kisses him goodbye, short. “Text me when you’re out.” Her hand stays on his sleeve after the kiss, his cuff in her fingers, and then she lets go of it.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 5:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL → 5:40 PM · THE FISHBOWL
body: Kevin’s text finds him on the fourth-floor landing, where the east stairwell keeps its one good bar: *CNN in the Fishbowl. Come down.* The landing window has gone from gold to a deep blue since the last time he looked. Sunset was at three minutes past five, and the building didn’t announce it.
He is a flight and a half from the second floor when the voice comes up the well. It is Laney’s, and it is low, which it never is, and it carries anyway.
“…don’t you dare tell him, Theodore. Not one —”

On the ground floor the fire door bangs, a kid with a laundry bag shouldering in from the dusk, and the sentence stops where it is. Two faces tip up through the rail of the second-floor landing. Jack has one foot down on the next step and leaves it there.
“Costigan,” Theo says. The blazer, the tie, no hitch at all. “Laney was briefing me on rush etiquette.”

Laney, in the Pi Lam hoodie with the hood up, looks at Jack for one breath and goes through the second-floor door into her own hall without a word. Jack takes the last flight down. Theo falls in beside him on the stairs.
“Never write the thank-you note before they’ve bid,” Theo says. “It reads as presumption. The lacrosse team will talk to you about stationery for an hour. I have, in fact, been talked to.”
“Good to know,” Jack says.
“Pi Lam has forms for the forms,” Theo says. “It’s fascinating. Laney has a binder.”
“Laney has a binder?”
“In *tabs*, Costigan.” Theo’s tie is perfect, and has been since breakfast. “I’d show you, but it’s privileged.”

In the Fishbowl the television is on CNN with the sound up, and the room has arranged itself around it without anyone deciding to. It is night in New York, and the same hour in Port-au-Prince. The screen has a studio, a map with one dot on it, and under the anchor the same few pictures in rotation, because they are the pictures there are. A white building folded down on itself, floor on floor. A street full of dust with people standing in the middle of it, because the middle of the street is the one place nothing can come down on them. A woman on a curb in a blanket, holding a phone away from her face and looking at it.
“Dude,” Doug says, once, and the *u* is one *u* long.

A correspondent says he has not been able to reach his own bureau since the afternoon. The lines are down. The anchor reads a statement from the White House, which says the President has been briefed and that help is being readied, and turns to a man from a relief agency and asks him how many. “Nobody knows yet,” the man says, slowly. “The lines are down. We simply don’t know.”
“We don’t,” the anchor says. “Anybody who gives you a number tonight is guessing.”
Jack’s hand has gone to the medal under his shirt.

Kevin is forward on the arm of the middle couch with his BlackBerry in both hands. Doug is standing; Jack has never seen him stand for a television program. Margot is in the armchair with her arms crossed and her Docs flat on the floor. Theo does not sit. He stands by the glass door in the blazer, since the Sigma Rho smoker is at six, with his eyes on the screen. In the doorway beside him Priya, crossing the lobby with her clipboard, has stopped with the pen up over the page.
“Quiet hours are suspended in the Fishbowl until further notice,” she says, to the clipboard. “I don’t have a form for that. I’m going to make one.” And goes on across the lobby.

“It isn’t the building, a lot of the time,” Kevin says. He is looking at the BlackBerry, not the screen, and the sunny has gone out of him; what is left sounds like a very good student. “The ones they pull out on day three. They talk to you. They’re fine. The muscle’s been dying under the weight the whole time, and it’s holding everything it let go of, potassium mostly, and when you lift the weight it all goes to the heart at once. They can die in the ambulance.” He swallows. “It’s called crush syndrome. I did my science fair on it. Armenia, 1988.” Doug looks at him. “Second place,” Kevin says.
“It sounds like a good project,” Jack says.
“It was a tri-fold,” says Kevin, and the old Kevin is there for a syllable, and gone.
“How long can somebody last under there?” Theo says.
He says it to the television. Kevin answers it the same way.
“Days,” Kevin says. “If they’ve got air.”
On the screen the white building comes around again in the same still.

“I gave this afternoon,” Margot says. “Partners In Health. They have been in the Central Plateau since 1987, they have clinics standing and people in them who speak Kreyòl, and they don’t have to arrive. Give there. Not to the Red Cross. Not to the Church.”
“Catholic Relief is the Church,” Kevin says, not looking up. “And they’re in Haiti.”

“Then I amend it.” Margot uncrosses her arms. “Not to the Church, except the part that was already there and has been for years. That part I’ll allow. I am still giving to Farmer. Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. You’d like him. Lena would *love* him.”

She hears it. She stops with her mouth a little open, and uncaps her pen, and writes something small in the notebook on her knee, and shuts the notebook on the pen. Jack keeps his eyes on the building on the screen.
“I had a Haitian roommate,” Doug says. “Ninth grade, at band camp. Pierre. His family’s in Delray. I don’t have his number. Why don’t I have his number?”
“Your mom will have his mom,” Kevin says.
“She’ll have his mom.” Doug says it like a lifeline, and has his phone out and is through the glass and across the lobby before the anchor has finished the sentence he was on.
Kevin’s BlackBerry buzzes in his hands, and he reads it out flat.

He reads the screen like a menu he already knows. “A press release,” he says, “from my father’s office, forwarded by somebody who was told to forward it. *Meridian Pictures will commit* — no figure, I notice — *said Richard Vance, president of production.* Second paragraph. That’s where the money keeps its coat on.” He holds the phone against his thigh and checks the Rolex. “Brooks has a list.”

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE CHURCH, THEN THE NEWMAN HALL
body: St. Brendan’s is Ash Wednesday full on a Tuesday night. Every pew under the hull of the ceiling, and students down the side aisle sitting on the floor with their backpacks between their knees, and townspeople Jack has never seen at a twelve-ten, a woman in hospital scrubs with her car keys still in her hand. At the Marian shrine the votive rack is lit nearly to the last row, and the heat of it comes off the brass, and somebody has propped a sheet of printer paper against the rail with HAITI on it in marker, and nothing under it, because there is nothing yet to write. A boy Jack knows from the Commons line kneels on the bare floor in a Lakers jersey. Two girls from the Thursday Bible study are holding hands in the side aisle. Up in the loft Gus Ferreira has the organ down so low it’s more floor than sound.

Fr. Osei comes out in his black clerical shirt and doesn’t go to the ambo. He stands at the foot of the sanctuary step with his hands folded. “We know very little tonight,” he says, “and I will not pretend we know more; we know that they are our brothers and sisters, and that the Mother of God does not need the telephone lines to be working.”
He steps aside, and from the second pew Lena leads the decade.
“The first Sorrowful Mystery. The Agony in the Garden.”

Her voice reaches the back without being raised. Two weeks ago it was in his ear every night, from her back steps, from behind her father’s register, from the river. Now it’s coming from the second pew, and he’s six pews back, and it’s for everybody. *Our Father*, and the church comes in under her, the old men out ahead and the students dragging behind, and then the first Hail Mary.

Julian is beside her, sitting back while the whole pew kneels, his hands loose between his knees. He doesn’t pretend. He has the second half by heart now, and when the church answers he answers too, low, a word behind everyone, careful with it.

Jack starts the first Hail Mary on his own count, quick, the Glenwood Avenue speed, Nonna’s, the words worn flat as a step. By the second Hail Mary he is on hers. Somewhere in the sixth he stops hearing it as her voice and hears it as the count. *Now, and at the hour.* A full church says it ten times, slower than he has ever said it, and on half an island under Cuba there are people under concrete in the dark, and Gus keeps the organ under all of them, a tune half the room could hum.

After the Glory Be, people say their intentions out of the pews, as they do on a Sunday when Father leaves room. For the people in the buildings. For the doctors. For the ones who can’t get a call through. For Father’s friend — that from Mrs. Fitch. The church answers every one, and the woman in scrubs says one Jack can’t hear, and the church answers that too.
Then Osei blesses them, and Gus brings the organ up for the first time and takes the hymn through once from the top, and the church sits and listens to it with its coats on.
At half past eight the Newman hall is folding chairs, the urn, a smell of burnt coffee and radiator, forty people in their coats, and Lena with a clipboard.

She has had it since before the decade. Clipped to it: the Catholic Relief Services page, printed in the office and still warm at one corner; a table schedule for tomorrow on the Commons Lawn, ten to five, two-hour shifts; a one-page cash-box protocol, numbered; the diocese’s number for the deposit, written in her hand along the top margin. She has a pencil through her hair and a second one behind her ear for when somebody walks off with the first. Peter Haddad, the Newman president, starts to say something about forming a committee. “Lena, do you want to —” “Yes,” Lena says, before he gets to what, and inside two minutes he is holding the end of the tape while she puts up the sign-up sheet, and asking her where she wants the chairs. Becca is at the urn with Kevin, setting out cups in rows of ten. Jack is by the wall with a roll of masking tape somebody handed him, and when Lena needs the wall she reaches past him for it. “Excuse me, Jack.” Her sleeve goes by his. She smells of the votive rack.

Julian comes in from the parking lot with two cartons of the parish’s empty coffee cans for collection jars and sets them by the urn, and when the urn’s spigot sticks he jiggles the switch twice without being shown, which is what it takes, and goes back out for the next load.
She gives the orders in a whisper.

She doesn’t raise her voice once. The hall is loud, everybody talking and the urn coming to a boil, and every time she has the next thing to say she says it lower, barely over her breath, and the whole room leans in to hear it.

Jack has watched her argue for five months, at tables and on roofs and down a phone line at one in the morning. He has never watched her do this. “Y’all, money. Not cans, not clothes. Cans sit in a warehouse in Miami. They need money.” Money to CRS, every dollar, by check or cash, and receipts written by hand. Two to a shift. The box never leaves the table and is never alone with one person. “Nobody makes change out of the box. If somebody needs change, they give the smaller bill.”

“Who has a car at nine tomorrow?” Peter does. “You take the box out to the Commons at nine and bring it back at five, and Mrs. Fitch has the key, and nobody else does.” Somebody who can letter is wanted for the sign; Kenzie can letter. Somebody with a folding table that isn’t the one with the broken leg; the one with the broken leg is Newman’s, and it goes in the closet with a note on it in Lena’s hand.
Kenzie Rourke, the cantor, puts her hand halfway up. “Can we go? Like — down there? My cousin did a mission trip to Honduras —”
“Not this week,” Lena says. “This week they need surgeons and money. We’re the money.”

Tyler Brandt has been waiting by the piano. “Brother,” he says to Peter, and then corrects course to Lena. “Before anything else — shouldn’t we have a holy hour? Exposition. All night, if we have to.”
“We just prayed,” Lena says. “Thursday, nine to midnight, the chapel’s yours. Put it on the sheet and ask Father.” Tyler writes it on the sheet, in capitals, and underlines it, and looks very happy.
Mrs. Fitch has a checkbook open on her knee. “I’ll bring lemon bars. A dollar.” She writes the check. “They’re worth two.”
“Lemon bars, Mrs. Fitch.” Lena writes it down.
A sophomore by the window wants to do a 5K. Somebody else wants a Facebook group. “Yes,” Lena says, to both, “after. Tomorrow is the table,” and they write their names down for the table instead.
Near the front a girl with a violin case between her feet puts her hand straight up, as if she’s in school. “I could play. At the table. People stop for a violin.”
“Name?”
“Clare. Dominguez.”
“Two to three, Clare. Thank you.”
Over at the urn Kevin is filling the reservoir out of a gallon jug, very carefully, for the whole time the girl is talking, and he goes on pouring a little after it’s full.

In the doorway of the office, at the side of the hall, Fr. Osei has the phone to his ear, his reading glasses off and swinging on their cord, and he puts the receiver down and picks it up and dials again, and listens, and puts it down.

Peter, beside Jack at the sign-up sheet, says it low. “He’s been calling a doctor in Port-au-Prince since five. A friend from medical school, from Ghana. Yaw. He works at a hospital down there.” He tears off a strip of tape with his teeth. “Nothing goes through.”
Osei comes to the doorway when the room is busy and looks at them all, the whole hall and the urn and the lemon bars, and somebody near him asks him how he is.
“I asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor,” Osei says. “He said he couldn’t spare a young priest.”
Mrs. Fitch laughs first, at exactly the size it needs, and the room follows her a little way, and Osei goes back in to the phone.

Kenzie comes past Jack with the poster board for tomorrow’s sign under her arm and the markers in her fist, and stops, and says it brightly, as if it were nothing. “Oceanography! I saw. Peter has all of Fenner’s old midterms, if you want them.” She goes on to the sign-up table, where Lena is standing with the clipboard, and props the poster board against the table leg at Lena’s feet. Lena’s pencil doesn’t stop.
Lena works down the sheet name by name, a tick for each. She reaches his.
“Jack. Wednesday, one to three. With Becca.”
At the urn Becca turns around with a stack of cups and waves the stack at him.
Lena’s pen waits on the next line. She is looking at the sheet. “We need hands. Who else can you bring?”

Ten of them are on the couch arms and the carpet folding the half-sheets for the table in thirds — CATHOLIC RELIEF SERVICES · HAITI EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE · EVERY DOLLAR — and stacking them in piles of fifty. Lena is on the end of the couch with her stack on the cushion beside her, running her thumbnail down every fold. Julian is on the floor at the other end with his own pile. Kevin is on the arm of a chair folding with hospital corners, which no one has asked him to do. Jack has the carpet by the coffee table and paper cuts on two fingers.

The room is quiet except for the paper. Earlier the anchor read out what the President said at the White House, that the country stands ready to help, and before that a woman from the Red Cross who said it was too soon to know, and said it three ways. Kenzie asks once if anyone minds the volume and no one answers her, and she leaves it. Lena hasn’t looked at the television since they started. She looks at the folds.

On the screen there are still photographs, one after another: a white wall come down across a street; a woman sitting on a curb with gray dust in her hair and on her arms; men with their bare hands in a heap of broken block. Over them, a reporter’s voice on a telephone line from Port-au-Prince, breaking up and coming back. He is standing outside a building that came down. There are people under it. Lena squares her stack on the cushion, edges even, and gets up and goes out of the room.

s06b.slug: TUESDAY · 9:34 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE BACK STEPS BY THE COURTYARD
body: The door at the end of the hall has a push bar and a square of glass with wire in it. Beyond it is the courtyard: the olive tree, the sprinkler head on its pipe that hasn’t worked since anybody can remember, the one bulb over the sacristy door, and the three back steps down to the flagstones.

Jack’s hand is on the bar. He leans on it, and the door gives, and the night comes in around the edge, January and the olive and somebody’s cigarette from the street. His mouth is already open on her name. He shuts it.

Lena is on the second step with her arms around her knees and her back to him. Julian is on the step below her, sitting sideways, with his shoulder against her shin. He isn’t talking. He is looking at the olive tree, and his mouth is shut.
After a while he takes his cardigan off, a dark green one with leather buttons, and reaches up behind him and puts it over her shoulders, and goes back to the olive tree.

Her hand comes off her knee and finds the edge of the cardigan and holds it closed at her throat. Out on the street a car goes by slow, looking for parking, and its lights go across the top of the wall and the olive and the step and are gone. Somewhere behind Jack in the building the urn clicks off.
The bar is cold under Jack’s hand. He stands there with the door open a foot and the January coming in over his shoes, not going out, not going back. He could cross the flagstones in four steps.

Julian sees him. Over her head, across the courtyard light, he finds Jack in the gap of the door and gives him a small nod, decent, with nothing in it Jack can find but *it’s all right*. Lena doesn’t turn around.
Jack lets the door come back on him slowly, all the way, so it won’t bang. He goes back down the hall, past the office and the phone, to the lounge, and sits down on the carpet, and folds flyers.

s07b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:40 AM · THE BRICK, THIRD FLOOR
body: In the lobby of the Pacifica Library the newspaper rack has today’s *Los Angeles Times*, and above the fold the National Palace in Port-au-Prince has come down: the long white building with the dome, the dome dropped onto the floors beneath it and the wings bowed in. The stack hasn’t been touched. On the television over the circulation desk CNN runs with the sound off, a street of gray dust and people standing in it, and the girl at the desk keeps her eyes on her scanner when he goes by.

Up on three the carrels are full and quiet in a way that isn’t only the library’s. She has a double one at the end by the window, the kind somebody knocked the partition out of, and she’s in his flannel with their book open: *Oceanography 1*, the one copy between them, hers, because the bookstore had one left on Monday and she bought it with the face she uses on bookstores. The syllabus says chapter two is week two. She is on chapter two.

“I read it at three in the morning,” she says. “Sol and Tomás and me on the floor in front of CNN till four. I had to know what it was.” She turns the book around to him. “So. Look. You’re going to need this anyway. Fenner said.”
It’s a map of the Caribbean with the sea floor colored in, and lines across it with small arrows on them. She puts her finger on one.

“This is the Caribbean plate. This up here is North America. They’re not crashing into each other — it’s not that kind. They’re sliding past. Sideways.” She puts her two hands together on the carrel, edge to edge, and slides one forward along the other. “Except they don’t slide. They stick. For a hundred years, two hundred, they stick, and all that time it’s loading up, and then one afternoon it lets go at once. Strike-slip. There’s a fault that runs right along under the city.” She takes her hands back. “No warning. It says that in bold. There isn’t any warning, ever, for this kind.”
“Will it do it again?”

“It already did. Aftershocks. For weeks, it says.” She opens the book again to a diagram, a long line with bright spots along it. “And the push doesn’t go away. It moves down the fault to the next place that’s stuck.” She taps the city on the map. “They built the capital right on top of it. Everybody does. San Francisco. LA. You build where the harbor is, and the harbor is where the ground came apart a long time ago.”
She closes the book on her pencil.
“I wish I didn’t understand it,” Skye says.

He has his own homework: the first half of *Frankenstein* for Hale by Thursday, one of eleven novels in fourteen weeks. She takes it out of his hands before he has it open, a used paperback with the creature on the cover, and turns to the title page, and reads it to him, every word where it was put, her voice gone down low for it:
*Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me Man, did I solicit thee / From darkness to promote me?*
She hands it back.
“That’s the line,” she says. “That’s the whole show.”
And she goes back to the plates.

For half an hour they work. She slips her shoes off under the carrel and puts her feet in his lap, and does her reading with a yellow highlighter she keeps capping and uncapping, and he reads Captain Walton writing home to his sister from the ice. At twenty past ten the highlighter stops. Her head comes down on his shoulder, heavy, and her breathing goes long and slow.

He doesn’t move. He reads forty pages with one hand, turning them with his thumb against the edge of the carrel — Walton and the stranger on the ice, then Geneva, a mother, a boy who wants to know how everything works — with her hair against his jaw and her feet warm on his leg, and she smells of the beach and of his own shirt. A girl at the next carrel recognizes her; he watches it happen, the double take and the quick glance at him, and the girl goes back to her own book.
At ten to eleven Skye wakes up on him with the seam of his sleeve printed on her cheek.
