body: The sheet of printer paper is still propped against the rail at the Marian shrine, but it isn’t blank under HAITI anymore. Since last night it has filled from the top down in ballpoint and Sharpie and one green crayon: first names, a town after some of them, a few with *mother* or *brother* in front. Near the bottom, in Kevin’s tidy printing, PIERRE (DOUG’S, BAND CAMP) — DELRAY.

The twelve-ten is usually eleven people and Mrs. Fitch. Today it is full to the side aisle, and the people at the back are standing in their coats. Fr. Osei comes out in the green. Before the opening prayer he says what the Mass is for, without ornament: for Joseph Serge Miot, Archbishop of Port-au-Prince, found this morning in the ruins of his offices, that he may rest in peace; and for everyone in that city who has not been found.

Joey Abruzzo, who has never read anything at less than the volume of a kickoff, reads the first reading quietly: a boy asleep in the temple who hears his name in the night, and goes to the old priest, and is sent back to bed, and hears it again. Kenzie sings the psalm without the piano, and the church sings the response back to her, ragged: *Here am I, Lord; I come to do your will.*

Osei reads the Gospel himself, standing straight to spare the leg, and when he comes to the last thing the disciples say he gives it no more weight than anything else in the chapter: *Everyone is looking for you.* The woman in the pew ahead of Jack puts her fingers against her mouth.

There is no homily beyond this. Osei comes down to the foot of the sanctuary step, where he stood last night, and says it with his hands folded. “Everyone in Port-au-Prince is will be calling a name into the dark tonight, and all I know to tell you is to pray that somebody answers, *Here I am*.” He goes back up to the altar.

For the intercessions Kenzie takes the sheet down from the rail and reads it through, name by name, as far as the paper goes. It takes four minutes. She reads PIERRE and then, because it says so, *band camp, Delray*, and the church answers him as it answers all of them.

The line goes up past his knees and Jack stays where he is. He says the old prayer Nonna taught him, the second time since Monday, with his eyes on the driftwood crucifix, and gets as far as *come at least spiritually into my heart* when Kenzie starts the communion hymn over his head. It isn’t the same thing. It is what there is, and the line goes on without him.

Mrs. Fitch, in her lanyard, reads the announcements from the lectern as she reads them every day. The table on the Commons Lawn is open until five. Checks to Catholic Relief Services, not to Newman. The church stays open tonight until midnight, for anyone who wants to come in. Thursday night, nine to midnight, the chapel is open for a holy hour, which Tyler Brandt would like it known was his idea; Tyler Brandt, in the fourth pew, looks at his shoes and beams.
Afterward Osei is at the door under the bell, as he is every day, and he isn’t saying *Akwaaba* to anyone. When Jack reaches him he says it low, before Jack has opened his mouth.
“Yaw is alive,” Osei says. “He is operating in a parking lot.”
“Thank God.”
“I have been, since five this morning.”

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot.

s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:10 PM · THE COMMONS LAWN, UNDER FERRER TOWER — THE NEWMAN TABLE
body: The table is the one with four legs. Two sophomores carried it over from the Newman courtyard at nine and set it down on the only level stretch of the Commons Lawn that the sprinklers miss, under Ferrer Tower, and the fog burned off at noon, and by ten past one the table has the look of a thing that has been there for years: Lena’s sign taped across the front in purple marker, a gray cash box in the middle, a coffee can for coins, and in a webbed lawn chair at the end Mrs. Fitch, with a cooler at her feet and a paper plate of lemon bars under plastic wrap and an index card in her own hand that says $1.

body.title: A sign, hand-lettered, taped to the front of the table
body.text:
HAITI
CATHOLIC RELIEF SERVICES
CASH OR CHECKS (CHECKS TO CRS)

body: Peter Haddad, who has had the box since nine, hands it across with both hands and lets his shoulders down. The box never leaves the table, he says, and change never comes out of it; she will know. He is back at five for the box. His MacBook stays behind, propped on the cooler with CNN.com on it and the sound off.
“Rule four,” Becca reads from the protocol card taped inside the lid, in Lena’s handwriting. “The box is never alone with one person.” She looks at Jack. “That’s us. We’re two.”

Becca is already in her place behind the cash box, in the St. Brendan’s Coffee & Donuts apron with the receipt book in the pocket and her clipboard flat on the table. She has her grandmother’s rosary wound twice around her wrist and her braid over one shoulder, and at her elbow a cigar box that rattles. “Change,” she says, and taps the lid. “Coins first. I made change for four hundred people at the Kootenai County Fair, and Lena says the box doesn’t make change, so I brought a box.”
“Hi, Jack!” She says his name like a thing that’s been settled and she’s glad of. She pushes the cigar box a few inches toward him. “You do the dollars. I’ll do the coins.”

It is lemon bars and dollars. A man from the dining hall in a hairnet puts five singles in the coffee can, one at a time, and goes back in to his shift. Two girls in Portolá sweatshirts put in a ten between them. A freshman tells Mrs. Fitch he can’t have a lemon bar because he’s allergic to lemons. “Then give Haiti a dollar,” Mrs. Fitch says, “and think about what you’ve done,” and he does. Becca writes each receipt in her round, careful hand, name and amount, and tears it off along the perforation, and gives it over with both hands. Ferrer Tower plays the quarter hour over their heads, a note or two flat.
“How’s your Nonna?” Becca asks, tearing off a receipt.
“She lit a candle Tuesday and won’t say who for.”
“That’s allowed,” Becca says. “That’s the best kind. I’m on it.”

On the cooler, CNN.com has something it can show. A slope of broken concrete, men in shirtsleeves, a rope, and a woman being passed up out of a gap in it, hand to hand, into the daylight. She is alive. Jack can see her blink.

Becca stops with a quarter in each hand. “Look at her,” she says. “They got her. I put Haiti in my Glory Be at breakfast, and again at lunch. It fits anywhere. It’s short.” She turns her wrist, and the rosary swings. “This was my grandma’s. Agnes. She gave it to me when I left for here.”

“We drive over to Kellogg every May,” she says. “It’s forty minutes from us, in the Silver Valley, and Grandma brings a thermos. She sits and has her coffee, because Grandpa Walt’s name is on the memorial there.” She says it as information. “He was in the Sunshine Mine in ’seventy-two, when it caught fire. And Grandma went up to the gate with the other families, and she said this” — the wrist again — “at the gate for eight days. Eight days. And on the eighth day they brought two men up. Alive.”
“So you never stop,” Becca says. “That’s what she says. You just never stop.”
A boy with a skateboard wants a lemon bar and holds out a five. She makes his change out of the cigar box, coins first, and tells him God bless.

Jack has been banding the morning’s twenties since the thermos. His thumb goes through the same one twice. “That’s the same one,” Becca says, gently, not looking up from the receipt book. “Start the stack over. It’s the first rule of cash.” He starts the stack over. Under the plastic wrap Mrs. Fitch has stopped straightening the lemon bars.

choices.text: *Fold Nonna’s twenty into the box.*
response: He takes out his wallet and finds the twenty he has carried since Glenwood Avenue, folded small and square, still faintly butterscotch. He counts it once. He lays it in the box on top of the others, flat.
“That’s a lot,” Becca says. Her pen has stopped over the receipt book.
“It was for a trip.”
She looks at him, and then she writes it up. “Who do I put?”
“Carmela.”
CARMELA R., and *$20.00 — with thanks*. She tears it off and gives it to him with both hands, and he folds it into the wallet where the twenty was.

choices.text: “Pray it for them, Becca. Right now.”
response: “Okay,” Becca says. She unwinds the rosary from her wrist and starts it where she stands, the beads going through her fingers and her lips moving, straight behind the cash box with the clipboard under her arm.

Partway through the third Hail Mary two freshmen want lemon bars. She sells them both, makes their change, writes the receipts and hands them over, lips still moving, and does not lose her place. Jack comes in on the second half of each one, under his breath, and minds the box.

choices.text: *Say nothing. Make change.*
response: He says nothing. A man in a UPS-brown jacket with a hand truck stops for a lemon bar and holds out a ten, and Jack counts his change out of Becca’s cigar box as his mother does at the St. Brigid’s bake sale: coins first, into the palm, the bills on top, so the hand feels the weight before it feels the paper.
“Thanks, man,” the man says, and walks off with a lemon bar in one hand and the change in the other, looking back at the laptop over his shoulder until the corner of the Brick takes him.

body: The Saab comes up the service road behind Ferrer Tower, where cars aren’t allowed, and stops with two wheels on the grass. Skye gets out in sunglasses and his flannel, cuffs rolled to the elbow, over a yellow sundress that ends a good way above the knee, and crosses the Commons Lawn in flats, straight at the table, not hurrying. A groundskeeper on a riding mower watches her the length of the lawn and lets the mower wander into a sprinkler head.

body.text: “You said if I want,” she says, at the table.
“I brought all of them,” she says, at the table, and lowers the sunglasses to look at him over the top.
“You told me where you’d be,” she says, at the table. “You just didn’t tell me to come.”

body: She holds her hand out across the cash box, palm up. “And you stole my Oceanography.”

It rode over from the Brick in his bag, on top of *Frankenstein*. He gives it back. She tucks it under her arm and looks down the table — the sign, the gray box, the coffee can, Mrs. Fitch in her lawn chair with the lemon bars on a paper plate under plastic wrap — and stops at Becca.

Becca is already on her feet. She has the apron off over her head before anybody has said a name: navy, ST. BRENDAN’S COFFEE & DONUTS across the bib in white, and over the pocket a coffee stain the shape of a continent not on any map yet. She holds it out. “You’ll want this. People give more to an apron.”
Becca, who has never watched television, studies her with frank and friendly interest. “Are you in Jack’s seminar?”
“He’s in my *car*,” Skye says. “Mostly in second gear.”
“Oh!” Becca says. “You’re Skye! I saw.” She holds the apron out the rest of the way. “You’re so pretty.”

Skye laughs, surprised into it, and takes the apron and puts it on over the flannel, and Becca goes around behind her to do the strings and talks the entire time. She doesn’t save any of it for later. She and Jack went out in the fall, till just before Thanksgiving. She prayed for him all through Christmas, that he’d be happy, and look. And she’s good, honestly, in case anybody was going to wonder — she has a lab section and a hermit crab. “Thomas. He’s not speaking to me.”
“What did you do to him?”
“Took him to Idaho. He saw snow.”
“I saw snow once,” Skye says. “Big Bear. I didn’t speak to my mother for a week.” She looks back over her shoulder at Becca working the knot. “He’s right.”
Becca laughs, a big, uncomplicated laugh, and pats the knot twice when it’s done.
At the cash box Jack makes change for a freshman buying two lemon bars, and gets it wrong, and counts it again, coins first, and gets it right.
Skye goes to work.

Three girls in matching Greek letters come along the walk toward the Commons, and she’s a carnival barker before they reach the sign. “Ladies! Ladies of Alpha Phi! A dollar gets you a lemon bar. Five gets you a lemon bar and my respect. *Twenty* — twenty, ladies — and the name of your sorority will be spoken with honor at this table for the rest of the afternoon, and *only* yours.” They give sixty, the three of them, and leave arguing about whether they were had.

The lacrosse team drifts by in a slow herd with their sticks over their shoulders, and she climbs up on Mrs. Fitch’s cooler — Mrs. Fitch moves the lemon bars — and turns into a livestock auctioneer at a county fair. “I’ve got ten, ten, do I hear twenty, twenty from the big fella, twenty-twenty-twenty, do I hear thirty, *thirty* from the *goalie*, gentlemen, I can see your wallets from here —” From the back the goalie, red to the neck, holds up a ten. A big one in a Marisol Lacrosse hoodie puts in a fifty and asks what she’s doing Friday. “*Sold*,” she says, “to the gentleman in the hoodie, for one lemon bar,” and hands it down to him, and he goes away happy.
For a boy in a tie, she drops into a clipped murmur, eyes on a screen that isn’t there: “*The network loves a nice boy.* Twenty dollars.” He pays it and straightens his tie.
Mrs. Fitch, who has sold lemon bars after Masses since the Johnson administration, watches all of it from her lawn chair, says, “Well,” and moves the plate down the table to Skye’s end.

Before long she and Becca have a system. Becca calls the coins and Skye calls the bills; Becca writes the receipts and Skye tears them off and gives them over with a line apiece, and whenever the twenties pile up Becca counts them without being asked and says, “Good,” to the money.
Two girls in Marisol Soccer sweatshirts stop dead on the walk, and one grabs the other’s arm hard enough to hurt. “Oh my God. Are you — *Cassidy*?”
Skye doesn’t even turn around. “Twenty dollars to Catholic Relief Services,” she says, “and Cassidy says your name.”

They have forty dollars on them. Skye takes it and folds it into the box and leans across the table to them, and her voice goes up half a step, soft and a little frightened, and it’s Cassidy, out of the television, on the Commons Lawn in a coffee apron.
“*Brittany*,” Cassidy says, as though Brittany is the bravest girl she has ever met. “*Courtney.*”
Courtney puts both hands over her mouth.

After that there’s a line. It comes out of nowhere, off the walk and out of the Commons doors and down the steps of the Brick — girls mostly, and some boys who are there for a friend — and Cassidy says *Ashley*, and *Megan*, and *Devin*, and Devin goes red to the ears, and *Lauren*, and the twenties come over the table faster than Jack can flatten them. By two the box won’t close over the bills.

Becca takes a parish envelope off her clipboard, writes SKYE on it in Sharpie, and starts banding the twenties in tens. “Box doesn’t leave the table,” she tells Jack. “The envelope’s still the table.”

Near the back of the line a girl lifts an iPhone over the head in front of her and holds it there. There’s no flash; in this sun there doesn’t need to be. From where she’s standing the box is in it, and so is the boy behind the box. Jack sees the phone come up. Between one name and the next, Skye sees him see it.

She doesn’t stop. She finishes the girl in front of her — “*Jenna*” — and says to the line, still in Cassidy’s voice, “Pictures by the tower, you guys. Not at the table. By the tower. Twenty.” And they go, in twos and threes, and stand under Ferrer with their arms around her. She leaves the table every few minutes to do it and comes back with the money, and every picture has the tower in it.
“Corinne’s going to love that,” Jack says.
“Who’s Corinne?” says Becca.
“My conscience,” Skye says. “She’s in Beverly Hills.”

At two, as Clare Dominguez is opening her violin case on the grass at the end of the table, Skye comes back from the tower with sixty dollars and the apron sliding loose at her back, and leans on the table beside him, hip to the edge, and looks from Becca to Jack with her eyebrows up, waiting to see what he’ll do with any of this.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall. The first day back, on the steps of St. Brendan’s, she said she saw, and she’s happy for me. Over Christmas she prayed I’d be happy. Thomas saw snow. At the Haiti table: her grandmother prayed that rosary at the gate of the Sunshine Mine in 1972, eight days. On the eighth day two men came up. She lent Skye her apron.

choices.text: “Becca and I went out in the fall.”
choices.key: At the Haiti table Skye borrowed Becca’s apron. You told Skye that you and Becca went out in the fall.
response: “Becca and I went out in the fall,” he says.
“And now we do lemon bars,” Becca says, first.
“I know,” Skye says. “She told me.” She tucks the sixty into Becca’s envelope and turns back to him. “She told me she prayed for you.”
Becca goes pink and sells a lemon bar to a boy who only wanted change.

choices.text: “Becca ran the Advent white elephant like a cattle auction. You’re up against a legend.”
choices.key: At the Haiti table Skye borrowed Becca’s apron. You told Skye she was up against a legend.
response: “Becca ran the Advent white elephant like a cattle auction,” he says. “You’re up against a legend.”
“Three steals and it’s frozen,” Becca says. “It’s just rules.”
Skye turns to Jack with the sixty dollars still in her fist. “I love her.”

choices.text: *Retie the apron for her. The knot’s come loose.*
choices.key: At the Haiti table Skye borrowed Becca’s apron. You retied it for her, in front of everybody.
response: He takes the strings at the small of her back, in front of the table and the line and Mrs. Fitch, and undoes Becca’s knot and ties it again, a square knot, the one his father uses on a tarp, pulled snug. Under the flannel she is warm through the cotton. She holds very still for it, and when it’s done she leans back into his hands, just slightly, before she steps away to the box.
Becca watches the knot, and then looks at the laptop.

body: Clare Dominguez has had her case open on the grass at the end of the table since two, and the Commons Lawn has done what she said it would. People stop for a violin. A man on a bicycle has stopped astride it with one foot down. Two girls with a blanket have given up deciding where to spread it and are standing on it folded. Clare plays with her eyes half shut and her chin down on the wood, a slow tune that sounds a hundred years older than it is, and when it ends Skye, at the box, says *again*, and half the lawn says it after her, and Clare plays it again, and the coffee can gets heavier. Skye stops calling names while it plays. She leans her hip on the edge of the table and listens with her head on one side and the twenties forgotten in her hand, and the girls in line wait for her.
Kevin comes across from the Commons with two flats of bottled water stacked against his chest, the shrink-wrap squeaking, and sets them under the table by Becca’s feet.
“You can’t send water,” Becca says.
“I know.” He straightens up. “It’s for the table.”

He doesn’t leave. When Clare stops to tune, he crouches by the open case and holds the lid back off the grass for her, though it stays back fine on its own, so the dollars people drop go on the velvet instead of the lawn.
“My mother knows your mother,” Kevin says.
Clare tightens a peg. “Everybody’s mother knows my mother.” She puts the violin back under her chin.
Kevin holds the lid.
At the cash box Skye bands a stack of ones and says to Jack, low, “He’s sweet.” She watches Kevin crouch there by the case until Clare starts again.

At half past Theo comes up the walk from the Commons with two Sigma Rho brothers ahead of him — one of them Brooks Callahan, the senior, in a visor, in January — and stops long enough to drop a hundred-dollar bill, folded in quarters, into the box. He gives Skye a small, correct nod.
“They liked my onion,” he says to Jack.
“So you’re in.”
“I’m in a climate. A bid is a separate weather system.”
Brooks wants a picture with Cassidy. So does the other one; he says his sister will die.
“A hundred each,” Skye says. “Cash. Not at the table, boys. By the tower.”

Brooks peels two hundreds off a fold and pays for both of them, and they go over to Ferrer and put her in the middle with their arms around her, and Theo goes along and stays over there in the shade of the tower after the pictures are done, talking to Brooks with his hands, laughing in the right places.

Yusuf comes by on his way to the Brick with his bag on one shoulder and pushes a wad of small bills into the coffee can. “From my father’s shop,” he says. “They passed a hat this morning.” He shrugs. “The line’s got weeks. They passed it anyway.”

At twenty to three Hale crosses the lawn on the diagonal, coat open, blue books under one arm, and drops a sealed envelope into the coffee can without breaking stride. “Tell Father Osei an atheist did this,” he says to Jack, already past. “He’ll be insufferable.”

Clare plays the slow tune a third time because a woman on the grass with a stroller asks her to. On Peter Haddad’s laptop, with the sound off under the violin, there is a crowd at a chain-link fence, and past it an airfield, and a gray cargo plane on the tarmac with its ramp down and nothing coming off it yet.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’

journal.title: Clare Dominguez
journal.text: Clare Dominguez. Newman sophomore. Plays violin in the Mass band. Played ‘Ashokan Farewell’ at the Haiti table and people stopped on the lawn. Kevin’s mother knows her mother. Everybody’s mother knows her mother.

body: The lawn empties out between classes. Clare has put the violin down to rest her bow arm, and Kevin has the closed case across his knees. On Peter’s laptop a man is standing in a street in Port-au-Prince holding up a photograph to the camera, a small school picture of somebody, and his mouth is moving, and the sound is off. He holds it up to the camera, and then he turns and holds it up to the street.
Skye has her sunglasses off and folded into the apron pocket. She watches the man with the photograph until the clip ends, and says to Jack, curious: “Where was God at 4:53?”
He looks at her.

“I’m asking,” she says. “I have the how.” She lifts the corner of the cash box and sets it down again on her Oceanography, which has been under it since two, keeping the ones from blowing away. “Two plates, one sliding past the other, a fault right under the city. It isn’t anybody’s fault. I read it twice. I want the where.”

“He isn’t one of the causes,” Jack says. “That’s the first thing. He’s not standing next to the fault deciding when. He’s the reason there’s a fault, and a city on top of it, and anybody in the city. He’s holding all of it up.”
“Including the part that fell down.”

“The ground that holds you up is the same ground that moves. You don’t get one without the other.” He knocks on the cash box, over her book. “Your chapter says the plates are why there’s land at all. Mountains. Rain off the mountains. A world where the ground never moves is a world where nothing does.” On the laptop men are pulling at broken block with their bare hands, passing the pieces back one to the next. “And where He is now is there. In the hands. In a parking lot in Port-au-Prince, where a doctor Father Osei went to medical school with is operating right now. At a card table on a lawn, even. He’s *there*.”
She listens to all of it with her elbows on the table and her chin in one hand, deciding whether to let him have it.

“Your G. K. doesn’t say that,” she says. “I’m past chapter seven. He says there was a minute on the cross when God seemed to be an atheist.” She sits back. “*My God, my God, why have you forsaken me.* He didn’t get the speech about the ground. He asked where. Your God asked where, Jack. Out loud. In front of His mother.”
“And He got an answer.”
“On Sunday.” She tips her head at the laptop. “It’s Wednesday.”

Jack opens his mouth, and she holds up a finger — wait — because a girl with a ten has come up to the table and is holding it out shyly, and Skye takes it and thanks her by her first name, which she gets off the girl’s sweatshirt, and turns back.
“That’s a beautiful answer,” Skye says. “To a question nobody under that building is asking.”
“So what are they asking?”
“*Is anybody coming.*”

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:55 PM · THE COMMONS LAWN → THE TABLE
body: Three people are crossing the grass from the direction of St. Brendan’s: Lena with her clipboard against her chest and a bundle of bank deposit envelopes on top of it; Laney beside her in sunglasses; and a few steps behind them, Julian, with a stack of yellow flyers under one arm. Jack sees them before they’re halfway. Lena has the gray cardigan buttoned to the throat in sixty-five degrees, and she comes straight across the grass instead of around by the path. The last time she was this close to him she was reaching past him for the wall. Skye has turned back to the box for a man in a bike helmet who wants to pay in quarters, and is counting them out for him in a librarian’s hush.
Laney says something to Lena. The wind is off the water, and it carries.
“Well. Somebody hand me my good manners. I’m fixing to need every one of them.”
Jack hears every word of it. Beside him Skye is still counting the bike man’s quarters out of his palm — *seventy-five, a dollar, and twenty-five*.

Lena looks at the girl in the apron. Then she looks down at her clipboard, and across the lawn Ferrer Tower starts in on the hour, off-key, and she writes the time — *3:00* — and the pen keeps going after the time is written, a line out along the margin, before she lifts it.
Laney gets to the table first. She takes her sunglasses off, looks at Skye from the flats to the apron to the hair, and puts them back on.
“Well, hey there,” she says. “Laney Price. I’d shake your hand, but I just did my nails for Haiti.”
“Skye.” Skye holds up both hands, full of quarters. “I’d shake yours, but I’m holding the Lord’s money.”
“I’ve seen your show.”
“Which episode?”
“The one with you in it.”

Laney opens her wallet — pink, a rhinestone L on the clasp — and takes out a hundred-dollar bill, and walks it down the table past the cash box and past the lemon bars to the far end, where Lena, arriving, has just set down her deposit envelopes, and lays it on top of them. “I’m giving to the clipboard.”
“*I’m givin’ to the clipboard*,” Skye says — in Dallas, Laney’s own Dallas, every long vowel and the little lift at the end, as if she grew up two doors down.
Laney laughs. It gets out of her all at once, and she shoves the sunglasses hard up her nose with one finger, as though that could put it back.
“Don’t do that.”
“Do what?”
“Be funny,” Laney says. “I’ve decided.”
She turns her back on the apron and beams at Becca. “Becca Lindell, you look precious.”
“Thank you!” Becca says. “Skye has my apron.”

“I can see that, angel.” Laney picks up a lemon bar, lays a five on Mrs. Fitch’s plate instead of in the box, and says, “Keep it, Mrs. Fitch. Buy yourself something lemon,” and Mrs. Fitch says, “I intend to.”

Lena clips the hundred to the top envelope and sets the clipboard down beside them. On Peter’s laptop, down the table in her sightline, the man with the school picture has come around again. Julian stops at the lemon-bar end with his flyers and says, “Hey, Jack,” with a nod, because his hands are full. Skye turns from the box with the quarters still in her hands, and Lena looks up from the clipboard, and the two of them are standing at the same card table, with Jack and the cash box in the middle of it.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard.

body: “Sugar,” Laney says, taking one, “I’ll be there Friday with bells on.”
“Thanks, Laney.”
Theo is coming back past the table, the brothers out ahead of him toward the Commons. He slows for Skye. “Callender, you’ve *raised money*. Your mother will be appalled.”

Theo takes a flyer off Julian’s stack and reads it and keeps hold of it. “Songs for Haiti,” he says, not quite under his breath. “How many are about her?”
Julian looks at him. He doesn’t seem offended by the question. He seems to think it deserves an answer.
“One.”
Theo folds the flyer into his shirt pocket and goes on after his brothers. Julian lays a stack of flyers at the end of the table, by Mrs. Fitch’s lemon bars, and squares it with the side of his hand.

A boy from Anacapa — the floor sweatshirt, a lanyard of keys — comes up the walk with a little silver Canon in one hand and a twenty in the other. “Can I get one? With the box?” He holds up the twenty. “It’s for Haiti.”
“No pictures at the table, please,” Lena tells him.

“Yes, ma’am,” Skye says at once, and comes around the table and turns the boy by the shoulder toward Ferrer, already in a museum audio guide’s voice — “*If you’ll proceed to the tower, you’ll find on your left* —” — and the boy goes with her.
It’s over. Jack hears himself say it anyway.
“It’s twenty dollars, Lena.”
Lena finishes the line she’s writing. She looks up.
“*Take care not to perform righteous deeds in order that people may see them,*” she says. “Matthew six. *Do not let your left hand know what your right is doing.*”
“I know what it says.”

“Then you know what I mean. There’s a city under a building, Jack. Those people aren’t a background. The ones under that concrete shouldn’t have to come with a picture of whoever’s holding the box.” She caps the pen. “Dorothy Day wouldn’t let the poor be an occasion. For anybody’s goodness. Ours either.”

“*Your light must shine before others,*” Jack says, “*that they may see your good deeds and glorify your heavenly Father.* Matthew five.” He doesn’t take his hands off the box. “The money doesn’t know who was holding it. A kid in Port-au-Prince gets water either way.”
“And the boy from Anacapa gets a picture of himself with a face off the television, and Haiti is in the back of it.”
“Haiti gets twenty dollars.”
“Haiti gets twenty dollars,” Lena agrees. “And a picture.”

“Half the windows at St. Brendan’s have a family’s name under them. Somebody paid for the glass and wanted it known. He sat across from the treasury and watched who put in what. Mark twelve. He *watched*.”

“And the one He praised was the widow with two coins,” Lena says, “and there wasn’t a soul in that temple who would have taken her picture.” She turns a page on the clipboard. “The people on that laptop have names, Jack. The man holding up the photograph has a name. Every one of them is somebody’s whole life, and they don’t owe anybody on this lawn a good afternoon.”
“There isn’t a person at this table having a good afternoon.”
“No,” Lena says. “I know.” And the pen goes on down the page.

They say all of it at an ordinary volume, across the lemon bars. Becca sells two lemon bars and makes change and sells another. Laney stands behind her sunglasses and doesn’t move. Kevin has Clare’s case shut across his knees and both hands on the lid. Over by the tower Skye has the boy from Anacapa by the elbow, laughing at something he’s said, and she has turned him so his back is to the table.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek. Kissed her goodbye at his car, for Oakland. Asked me to make sure she eats before her flight. In sixty-one pictures from Lucille’s baptism, at the Broussards’ table between Mémère and Josie. Tess’s caption calls him *le petit violon*. Flew home to Oakland on the fourth. Tuesday morning, on the feed: a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late; Lena tagged. Songs for Haiti, Friday at Bastille, every dollar to CRS. Theo asked him how many are about her. ‘One.’

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:10 PM · THE SAAB, THE BLUFF ROAD
body: The sun has gone into the water by ten past five, but the sky is still lit from underneath: orange along the bottom and then a long clean blue going dark at the top, and the Saab is parked on the bluff road with its top down and its nose at all of it.

Her phone goes off on the dash. She looks at the name and lets it ring. She takes his hand off his knee and puts it on the gearshift and puts hers over it, and leaves them there through three more rings, and then she answers on speaker.
“I’m looking at you in an apron,” Corinne says.
“It’s Becca’s.”

“I don’t know who Becca is. There are eleven pictures of you on a *Sweetwater* fan forum and four on TwitPic — plus one from yesterday from a *lecture hall*, Skye, which I didn’t know you attended — and the forum ones have a caption — *Cassidy says your name* — with three exclamation points. That’s in two hours. It’s adorable.” A keystroke in Beverly Hills. “It is also not managed. I have a statement. ‘Skye is heartbroken by the devastation in Haiti and was proud to —’”
Skye says the next part along with her, silently, with her eyes shut, and gets every word.
“— and there’s a boy at the back of every one of them,” Corinne says.
“He was holding the cash box.”

body.text: “Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. He *commented*. ‘Hi, Glenwood Ave.’”
“Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. He deleted one, and a man named Tommy put it back with *lol*.”
“Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. His friend count went up by twenty-three in an afternoon. Who *are* these people?”
“Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. Forty-seven comments under a video of my client, and he hasn’t touched it. Tell him I said good.”

body: Jack looks at the phone. Skye looks at Jack, and for the first time since it rang, her mouth goes up at one corner.
“The network called me at three,” Corinne says. “They wanted to know who the boy is. I said a friend from school.”
“He’s not a friend from school.” Skye picks a fleck of bark off the dash and flicks it over the side. “He’s a boyfriend from school. It’s in the system, Corinne. I put it there.”
“I’m aware of where it is.” Another keystroke. “And thank you for taking down the car.”
“Not for you.”
A click on the line, and another voice, warmer and farther off: Debbie, on the extension in Studio City. “Baby, people want to see you care.”

“I cared for an hour in an apron, Mother.” Skye opens her eyes. “It’s twenty-dollar bills, Corinne. You can’t release twenty-dollar bills.” And then: “The girl at the table said no pictures. She was right.”
There is a silence in Beverly Hills long enough to hear the surf come up the bluff.
“We’ll talk tomorrow,” Corinne says.
“We will,” Skye says, and hangs up, and doesn’t move her hand. His is still under it on the gearshift. He turns it over, so her fingers lie in his palm.

Below the bluff the tide is going out over the reef, white where it breaks and then dark, and a pelican goes along the line of it low enough to touch. They stay till the color is gone and the platforms come on out on the black water, one and then another. She asks him what the creature wants yet, and he says he’s only as far as Geneva, and she says the creature wants what everybody wants and she isn’t going to tell him what that is until he’s done. She tells him about the table from her side of it: a girl named Brittany who cried when Cassidy said her name, and gave forty instead of twenty, and asked if Cassidy was going to be okay at boarding school. “I made a Brittany cry for Haiti,” Skye says. “I’m not proud. I’m a little proud.” She looks at him sideways. “You were good at the box. You count money like a nun.”
“My mother counts money like a nun. I count it like her.”

“Same thing, then,” she says, and puts her feet up on the dash. At eight she drives them to Lupe’s truck, and they eat carne asada out of foil in the car with the dome light on, and she gets salsa on the cuff of his flannel and says it’s hers now anyway.
Halfway through the carne asada the RAZR goes off on his knee. It’s eleven at night on Glenwood Avenue.

body.title: A sign taped to the church door
body.text: OPEN UNTIL MIDNIGHT FOR HAITI. COME IN. —Fr. G.

body: St. Brendan’s has its doors propped and most of its lights off. The coat-closet confessional at the back is dark, its KNOCK (gently) card turned to the wall. Up the nave the hull of the ceiling goes away into shadow over the pews, and the blue glass is black, and the only real light is at the Marian shrine on the right, where the votive rack is nearly full — three tiers of small flames in red glass — and the light from it moves on the wall. Four people are praying, scattered, one to a pew. At the far end, by the sacristy door, Father Osei is turning off a light. He sees them, and goes through the door, and leaves them be.
Skye stops just inside with her hand on the back of the last pew. She has never been inside a Catholic church at night, and she tells him so in a whisper.
“I’ve shot in three,” she whispers. “Day for night. There was craft services in the confessional.”

He takes her up the side aisle to the rack. She wants to light one; she has never lit one. He shows her: the long taper out of the sand tray, a flame borrowed from somebody else’s candle, the wick, the taper back in the sand. The slot wants money. She has a twenty and nothing smaller; he has four quarters he was saving for the dryer, and two of them go in, and she listens to each one land.
She lights it with both hands on the taper and doesn’t breathe until it takes.
Under the shrine, in the moving light, there is the brass plate. She bends to read it.

body.title: A brass plate under the shrine
body.text: NORA GRACE CALLOWAY · 1989–2009 · “LORD, TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?”

body: “Who was she?”

He tells her what everybody knows. A sophomore; a soprano; she sang in this choir. She went out to the Point one night last April and fell from the wall. It was in the paper. Newman put the plate up in the fall.
Skye looks at it, and draws the taper out of the sand again. “For her too,” she says, “since I’m here,” and lights a second one beside the first, and he feeds the slot the last two quarters.
They stand there. Somebody at the back opens the door to leave and the night comes up the aisle, and every flame in the rack leans and comes back.
Up by the altar, in the dark, one lamp is burning that isn’t at the shrine: a small red glass on a chain beside the tabernacle. She has seen it. She points with her chin.
“Why is that one red? It’s the only one up there.”
“It means He’s there.”
“Who?”
“Him. In the tabernacle. The bread from Mass.” He doesn’t lower his voice any further than it already is. “It stays lit as long as He’s in there. It’s somebody’s job to make sure it never goes out.”
She looks at the little red lamp a long time, with her arms folded inside his flannel. “You think that’s really Him. In a box. In a building in Santa Barbara, with the lights off.”
“Yes.”
“What’s that like?” She isn’t asking what he believes. She’s asked that before. “Knowing it’s in there.”
He tries. “Like coming home and the porch light’s on. You don’t look at it. You’d know if it was off.”

s13b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:20 PM · DEL PLAYA, THE PORCH
body: The porch at Sol’s house leans toward the sea; it always has. The swing hangs off it on two chains with every blanket off her bed piled on it, and his Carhartt on top. Tomás’s boards stand against the rail. The heater inside is still broken, and it’s warmer out here than in. Through the front window Sol’s television is on CNN with the sound off, Haiti going all night in a lit square behind their heads, and from somewhere deeper in the house, on Sol’s record player, a woman is singing low over a drum machine and something like strings.

Her room is through the door and down the hall. They don’t go in. She sits down on the swing and he sits down beside her, and she pulls the blankets up over both of them, and the swing moves under them and settles.

She doesn’t sleep. She sits with her knees up under the blankets and her chin on them, and watches the screen through the glass over his shoulder. Without any sound, men in a street of gray dust are pulling at a slab of concrete with their hands. The picture changes to a man on a phone, and back to the slab.

Sol made a pot of rice last night at nine, she tells him, because Sol’s mother makes rice when something terrible happens, and none of them ate it, and at two in the morning all three of them ate it standing up out of the pot. “It was very bad rice,” Skye says. “I had seconds. Sol can never know.”
Her legs come across his lap under the blankets, and her feet find the warm place against his hip and settle there. She’s in his flannel still, with the salsa on the cuff.

body: “With her. You ask her to pray with you.”
“So she’s your agent.”
“Agents take ten percent.”
“What does she take?”
“Nothing. She just asks.” He thinks about how to say the rest. “She’s the one who stood there. At the end. When everybody else ran.”
Skye watches the slab through the window. “She stood there,” she says. “I can see why you’d want her in the room.”
Inside the house the record turns over to something slower.

“I called her back,” Skye says. “My mother. At six this morning. I said I was sorry I hung up.” She pulls the blanket up to her chin. “She said, baby, I’ve been hung up on by better. And then we watched it together on the phone for ten minutes, her in Studio City and me here, and neither of us said anything clever.” She’s quiet. “That was nice. Don’t tell her I said nice.”
“What do you pray,” she says. “For people under a building.”

s13c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD → THE SAAB
body: Out in the courtyard the olive tree has the streetlight caught up in it, and the sprinkler stands in the dead grass with its head cocked, as it has all year. She sits on the edge of the planter under the tree and pulls him down next to her by his sleeve.
“Tell me who everybody was,” she says. “At the table.”
So he tells her. Becca, from Idaho, who lent her the apron.
“I know. She told me. I want to adopt her.”
Clare, with the violin, a sophomore at Newman. The guy who brought two flats of water you can’t send anywhere, and stayed to hold the case.
“Kevin. From the glass room. He held it like it had a baby in it.”
Theo, and Theo’s onion.
“Ted. I could smell it from the box.”
The redhead in the sunglasses.
“Laney. She introduced herself.” Skye stretches her legs out on the flagstones. “She hates me. I’m going to get her a present.”
And the guy with the flyers.
“Songs for Haiti,” Skye says. “I read the flyer.”
He gets to the end of the table and stops there. Skye doesn’t ask. She reaches up and turns his medal right side out where it had flipped on its chain, and leaves her fingers on it a little.
On the way out through the gate she looks back at the church, at the doors still propped and the red light in the side windows. “Can you buy those? The candles. Can you buy a box of them somewhere?”
“Not those ones. Those live here.”
“So I’ll come back,” she says, and takes his hand to cross the street.
At the Saab, under the streetlight on Ocean Road, she leans back against her door with her hands in the front pocket of his flannel, and takes them out.
“I want to take you home,” she says. “I want that a lot. And I’m too sad tonight to be any good at it.”
She looks at him under the light.
“Saturday.”
The streetlight buzzes over them. Somewhere down Ocean Road a car alarm starts and gives up. “It’s in my calendar,” she says. “In pen.”
“And I wrote your brother. In capitals.” She pokes him in the chest. “I need the address.”

body: The lobby is down to its night lights. On the front desk Marcus’s radio is turned low to KCLU, a man on a bad line from Port-au-Prince and then a woman in a studio saying his name, and behind the desk Lena and Priya have the gray cash box open between them, and Priya’s CASH LOG, laminated, with a wet-erase marker on a string. The door of the RA safe under the desk stands open.

“Per the Residential Life Handbook,” Priya says, without being asked, because he’s standing there, “cash in excess of five hundred dollars does not sleep in a student room, Costigan. It sleeps in my safe.” She taps the laminate. “I made a log.”
“That’s in the handbook?”
“It is now.”

Lena signs the log. Priya countersigns it, and caps the marker, and uncaps it, and they count it once more together, the stacks laid out on the desk blotter: the ones and the fives, the tens, the checks under a binder clip. Lena does the twenties last. There is purple marker down the side of her hand, and a day of giving orders under her breath has left her almost no voice at all. She counts the twenties in a whisper anyway, every one, and Priya’s lips move with her. On the radio the man in the studio says the archbishop of Port-au-Prince again, found in the ruins of his offices, and Lena’s hands stop on the stack. Then they go on, and she starts the stack over from the top.
Lena finishes the count before she looks up. She turns her clipboard around on the desk and pushes a pen across to him with it. “You had the box from one to three. Initial your shift.”
He initials it under Becca’s *B.L.* She turns the clipboard back around.
“Four thousand eight hundred and seventeen dollars and forty cents.” She bands the twenties. “It goes in the safe tonight and to the diocese office at nine. Your table did the most.”
She lays the banded twenties in the box, and takes out one envelope that is fatter than the rest, and puts it back in again. “Skye’s envelope was the biggest. Tell her thank you. From Newman.”
Her hands are already closing the lid.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’

s14a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:42 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He goes back out the way he came in and sits down on the front steps. The quad is dark. Ferrer Tower is done chiming for the night, and the bike racks are full, and somebody’s sprinkler out by the lot is ticking around on the grass.

His bag is on the step beside him. In the front pocket, the tin: eleven, her count. In the side pocket, his own pack, as it rode home. Monday, on the back steps of Hollis, he put it back in the bag and zipped the pocket. Through the glass behind him the desk is empty now, and he can still hear the count, every twenty, in what was left of her voice. His thumb finds the lighter in his coat pocket and stays on the wheel.

choices.text: *Light one. Your own.*
response: He takes one out of his own pack and lights it with his shoulder to the quad. The smoke goes up past the dark windows of four and comes apart there. It doesn’t help. He smokes it to the filter anyway and puts it out on the step and puts the end in his pocket.
Monday he put it back. Tonight he didn’t.
The front door is heavy, and he lets it be heavy. Inside, the radio on the desk is still on Haiti, and he goes in past it.

response: He puts the pack back in the side pocket and runs the zipper shut. Somebody laughs out in the lot, two people, and a car door, and the sprinkler comes around again.

response: He opens the tin on his knee, under the light from the lobby, and counts them with one finger.
Eleven.

s15.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body: He left his charger in the lounge outlet this morning, the only live one on four that Theo’s power strip doesn’t own, and at ten to eleven, with the RAZR down to its last bar, he goes up to get it.

The lounge door is propped on its rubber wedge, the way Priya hates, and the light comes out across the hall carpet in a long bar. On the sill inside, Laney’s pink iPod dock is doing Lady Antebellum, low. His hand is on the frame when the song drops into its quiet part, and two voices come through the gap with nothing in the way.
“…the laptop’s in my closet, Theodore, and it’s staying there. And you can stop *nodding* at people —”
“It was a correct nod. It had the correct number of degrees.”
“Well, go sit with her.”
He pushes the door the rest of the way.

The lounge is what it is at eleven on a school night: every light on, the vending machine humming its one note in the corner, a pizza box on the radiator with one crust in it. Laney is on the window seat beside her dock with her knees up and the Pi Lam hood up, her phone in both hands, the nails red and blue, done for Haiti this afternoon, and the left thumbnail chewed through the polish. Theo is standing in the middle of the carpet in the rush blazer, back from the bluff or about to go there, with his hands in his pockets. Kevin is on the couch with a chemistry text across his knees and one earbud in. Margot is in the armchair with her Docs up on the coffee table and her notebook open on her knee, because Margot doesn’t sleep, she counts.

Behind her the whiteboard stands on its wheeled stand where it always stands, Margot’s by annexation: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, in her capitals, and under it COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD over a column of her marks, months old and never wiped, because she says it’s a record. Priya’s laminate is still taped to the frame.
Laney sees him. She turns the iPod down one notch, and then, looking at the window, up two.
“Costigan,” Theo says. “Good. You’re just in time to watch me be shunned.”
“Nobody’s shunning you, Theodore,” Laney says, thumbs going. “I’m keeping it short.”
“Since Sunday,” Theo says. “Texts only. Third person. I get *he* and a verb.”
“It’s Amish,” Margot says.
Kevin takes the earbud out. “Respectfully,” he says, before anyone has asked, “I was here first. I live here. I have a quiz on Friday.”
“He also has a violinist,” Margot says, and turns a page.
Kevin puts the earbud back in, and takes it out again. “I *met* a violinist. At a table. For Haiti. Our mothers know each other.”
“Everybody’s mother knows her mother,” Margot says. “You told us. Twice, at dinner, and once in the elevator, to a stranger.”
Kevin looks at the chemistry. “It was a long elevator,” he says.

Upside down from where Jack is standing, across the top of her open page, there is a name in capitals: SKYE. A Res Life flyer is folded into the gutter beside it with a line on it in Theo’s hand, and Jack can read that upside down too: THE ROSE IS A PLANT.

“To be clear,” Theo says, “I put a hundred dollars into a box for Catholic Relief Services, and Brooks bought two photographs with a television actress at a hundred apiece, also for Catholic Relief Services, and I nodded at her. Correctly. If anyone would like me to boycott the Red Cross as well, I’ll need it in writing.”
Laney doesn’t look up. “I’d like you to know whose side you’re on.”
“I’m on the side of the box.”
She looks up then, not at Theo. At Jack. Then back down to the phone, and her thumb goes on with whatever it was doing.
The charger is in the outlet behind Kevin’s couch.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’

response: “Mrs. Fitch will be thrilled,” says Theo.
Laney, to the ceiling: “*Lord.*”
He reaches behind the couch for the charger, and Kevin leans forward to let him.
Theo checks the Rolex. “I’m expected on the bluff at eleven,” he says. “They’re handing out envelopes, or drowning people. It’s unclear.” He goes past Jack in the doorway without stopping.
“Night,” Laney says, without turning her head.
It is the first word she has said to him since Sunday. He says it back to the top of her hood, and goes. Behind him the song comes around to the beginning again, and somebody turns it up.

body: Theo comes in with the rush blazer over his arm and hangs it in the closet as though it will be inspected in the morning. He props a card against the base of his lamp and steps back to look at it.

body.title: A card propped against Theo’s lamp
body.text:
SIGMA RHO
requests the honor of
Theodore Ashby Vance

body: “Congratulations,” Jack says from his bed.

“They want me,” Theo says. “It’s very flattering. They also want me to shave a lacrosse stick.” He sits on the end of his bed to unlace his shoes. “Brooks would like it known that he paid for two pictures this afternoon. I’ve told him charity is its own receipt, and he’s taking it to the chapter.”
“What’s a chapter?”
“Eleven men in a basement deciding what I’m worth. I came in third, behind a boy from Encino and a keg.” He takes off the Rolex and lays it face-up on the nightstand.

“Laney’s still keeping it short,” he says, to the watch. “Today’s texts, in full. Eleven in the morning: *a girl at the brick says she fell asleep on him.* Ten to two: *the saab is on the service road.* That’s the whole correspondence. You saw the rest. It’s a club now, Costigan. We should get jackets.”
“She’ll come around.”

“Laney doesn’t come around. Laney arrives.” He lines the watch up with the edge of the nightstand. “I’m not going to be rude to Callender in an apron for Haiti. I’ve known her since the Meridian lot. She was a very bad Cinderella and a very good stepsister.” He considers the lamp. “She looked happy today. I noticed that. I’ve noticed a lot of people this week who looked happy, and a few who didn’t, and I’m keeping a list, because nobody asked me to.”
“Who’s on it?”
“Goodnight, Costigan.”
He turns the lamp off, and the card goes dark with it.
The RAZR lights on his chest.
